passage: Monday. Gurleen invited Kishore to the gurdwara on Saturday for Baisakhi. Kishore asked Mummy first, and she smiled and told him to go and listen well. Saturday. Gurleen handed him a scarf for his head and whispered what each thing was: why everyone sits on the floor, what the warm sweet prasad is, why they all eat together in the langar. Kishore folded his hands the way Gurleen did and felt welcome. Monday. At school he told a classmate about the prasad. "Did you pray too?" the classmate asked. "I listened," Kishore said. "My own prayers are still mine. But I liked being there."

qa.q: What did Gurleen hand Kishore at the gurdwara?
qa.a: Gurleen handed him a scarf for his head.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel at the gurdwara, and what shows he was not worried about his own faith?
qa.a: He felt welcome; afterwards he said his own prayers were still his, but that he liked being there.

qa.q: How can a child join a friend's festival with respect and still keep their own faith?
qa.a: Listen, follow the customs politely, ask questions, and stay clear that joining does not mean having to agree, as Kishore did.

qa.q: How might Gurleen have felt showing Kishore around?
qa.a: Probably glad and proud to share, since Gurleen whispered patient explanations of each thing 🙂.

grounding: Illustrates a child welcomed to a friend's festival with patient explanations, joining respectfully without feeling threatened.

passage: The parish hall in Pune glowed with paper stars, and Darshan hovered at the door, unsure where to stand. Francis, beaming under his new haircut, grabbed his arm. 'You came! Come and sit with my family.' During the service Francis whispered explanations: 'That's the crib, with baby Jesus. Now everyone stands. You don't have to sing if you don't know it.' Darshan stood when they stood and folded his hands the way he did at home. When people went up for communion, Francis said, 'That part is only for us. Stay here with Mummy, she'll keep you company.' Afterwards, over plum cake, Darshan said, 'It's different from our Ganpati puja, but the feeling of everyone together is the same.' Francis's mother smiled. 'Come every year.'

qa.q: What did the parish hall glow with?
How did Darshan feel as Francis explained things?
qa.a: Welcomed and more at ease after hovering unsure at the door.
He stood when others stood, folded his hands as he did at home, and stayed back during communion, without needing to share every belief.

qa.q: How did Francis's mother see Darshan's visit?
qa.a: Warmly; she smiled and invited him to come every year.

grounding: A boy invited to his friend's Christmas service feels welcome as the friend explains, and joins respectfully without needing to agree.

passage:
Thursday. Thomas handed Bidisha an envelope with a hand-drawn egg on it. 'Easter lunch at our place, Sunday. Amma says you have to come.' Bidisha felt a flutter: she had never been to an Easter anything.
Sunday. Thomas met her at the gate and explained everything patiently. 'We went to church this morning, that's why Appachan is still in his white shirt. The eggs are for new life. Want to help hide them for the little ones?' At lunch his grandmother said a short prayer. Bidisha bowed her head politely and didn't pretend to say the words. Nobody minded. She felt welcome all the way through the appam and stew.
Monday. Bidisha told Ma, 'Their prayers are different from ours. But I didn't feel I had to change anything. I just felt invited.'

qa.q: What was drawn on Thomas's envelope?
How did Bidisha feel at Thomas's Easter lunch?
qa.a: Welcome and comfortable, all the way through the appam and stew.
She helped hide the eggs and bowed her head politely during the prayer without pretending to say words she didn't share.

qa.q: How did Thomas make Bidisha feel included?
qa.a: He explained each thing patiently and gave her a job hiding eggs.

grounding: Over several days a girl invited to her friend's Easter lunch feels welcome and joins respectfully without feeling her own faith is threatened.
